1:1: The author is using David to represent him and his men. See the discussion of this usage in the Introduction to 2 Samuel.
Here the name of a person, Amalek, represents his descendants.
See the discussion of the term “strike” in the Introduction to 2 Samuel.

The author is expressing this in the way his culture reckoned time. He does not mean that David and his men arrived in Ziklag and stayed there for two subsequent days before something further happened. He is reckoning the day of their arrival as the first of these two days.
1:2: In this culture, the current day was considered the first day, the next day was considered the second day, and the day after that was considered the third day. So this phrase is referring to the day after the day after David returned to Ziklag.
This was a symbolic action that showed the man was in mourning.
He knelt down in front of David as a gesture to honor him. He then prostrated himself or stretched out flat on the ground to show David great honor.
1:3: David is using a common expression of his culture.
1:4: By the people, the young man means the Israelite army.

The verbs fallen and died together also express a single idea. The verb fallen tells in what way these soldiers had died. Specifically, this was by being mortally wounded in battle, which caused them to fall to the ground.
1:9: The young man claims that Saul spoke of agony as if it were a living thing that could have seized him. This could mean: (1) that Saul is in such pain from his wounds that he is no longer capable of fighting. The agony would be restraining him in that sense, as if it had seized him and was holding him immobile; (2) that Saul has an overwhelming sense of pain.

This could mean: (1) that Saul is using a common expression of his culture to mean that he wants this young man to use violence against him. In this context, the expression stand over me may be equivalent to the expression “rise up against” in 22:49; (2) that Saul actually wants the young man to stand over him and use all of his weight to push a sword or spear into him and kill him.
By my life {is} still whole in me, Saul means that he is badly wounded, but not mortally wounded. He will not die imminently from the wounds he currently has.
1:10: The young man is using a common expression of his culture, I stood over him, to mean that he attacked Saul.

The young man does not mean that Saul had actually fallen to the ground. He says in 1:6 that Saul was standing up, leaning on his spear. The young man is speaking of Saul being badly defeated by the Philistines as if Saul had fallen from a height.

A crown is a decorative headpiece that shows that a person is a king. In this context, the term describes a narrow band of gold encircling Saul’s helmet, not a large, ornamental headpiece with jewels. The band on his arm was probably a decorative item worn on the arm to show that the person was a king.
1:11: This was a symbolic action that showed David was feeling shock and grief.
1:12: By the people of the Lord, the author means the Israelite army.

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Israel figuratively means all the people descended from the man named Israel (who was also known as Jacob).
The author is using the term fallen by association to mean that they had died, since soldiers fall down when they die.
The author is using the term sword by association to mean battle, since swords were used in battle.
1:13: David is using a common expression of his culture.
1:14: אֵיךְ לֹא יָרֵאתָ לִשְׁלֹחַ יָדְךָ לְשַׁחֵת אֶת־מְשִׁיחַ יְהוָה
David is using the question form for emphasis.
David is using a common expression of his culture, stretch out your hand, to mean attacking or violently harming someone.
1:16: This could mean: (1) that David is speaking to the Amalekite even though he cannot hear him (since he is already dead) in order to show in a strong way how he feels about his claim that he killed Saul. He would actually be speaking to the people who can hear him, the men around him. (The author’s statement in the previous verse, “and he died,” would be a description of what ultimately happened.)
David is using the term blood by association to mean “death,” since the young man he summoned shed the Amalekite’s blood when he killed him.
When David says on your head, he is using a common expression that means that someone is morally and legally responsible for something.
David is speaking of the young man’s mouth as if it were a living thing that could testify against him.
1:18: See the discussion of the phrase sons of in the Introduction to 2 Samuel.
1:19: David is speaking to the nation of Israel as if it were a person who could hear him. He is doing this to show in a strong way how he feels about the deaths of Saul and Jonathan. He is actually speaking to the people who can hear him, the people of Judah who will eventually learn this song.
David is using the term fallen by association to mean “died,” since these soldiers fell down when they died.
1:20: Following the customary practice of Hebrew poetry, David is using two phrases together that mean basically the same thing.
Here the term daughters has the same kind of meaning as the term sons in 1:18.
1:21: הָרֵי בַגִּלְבֹּעַ אַל־טַל וְאַל־מָטָר עֲלֵיכֶם וּשְׂדֵי תְרוּמֹת

David is speaking to the mountains of Gilboa as if they could hear him. He is doing this to show in a strong way how he feels about the deaths of Saul and Jonathan on those mountains. He is actually speaking to the people who can hear him, the people of Judah who will eventually learn this song.
1:22: David is speaking of the bow of Jonathan as if it had been a person who could have been sent to fulfill a task but who might have decided to turn itself back and not complete it. David is speaking similarly of the sword of Saul as if it had been a person who could have been sent to get something but who might have returned with empty hands, that is, without it.
David is speaking as if the bow and sword were living things that could drink blood and consume fat.
David is using the term bow by association to mean the arrows that Jonathan shot from his bow.
1:23: David is making an overstatement for emphasis.
1:24: David is speaking to the women of Israel as if they could hear him. He is doing this to show in a strong way how he feels about Saul’s death. He is actually speaking to the people who can hear him, the people of Judah who will eventually learn this song.

Saul had not directly clothed the Israelite women in scarlet, and he had not directly put gold ornaments on their clothing. David is illustrating the prosperity that Saul brought to Israel by ensuring its security and by plundering its enemies.
David is using the term scarlet by association to mean clothing that was scarlet in color.

This expression conveys a single idea by using two phrases connected with with. The phrase in delights tells in what way Saul clothed the women in scarlet. Specifically, the clothing brought delight to the ones who wore it.
The term scarlet refers to a bright red color. In this culture, people had to use an expensive dye to make clothes this color. So having scarlet clothing represented prosperity and status.
1:25: As in 1:19, the word your refers to the nation of Israel as if it were a single person.
1:26: David is speaking as if he were in a narrow (tightly confined) space in which he did not have much freedom of movement. In such a situation, a person would feel distress, and that feeling is what David is expressing through this image.
David is speaking as if Jonathan were his actual brother, even though he was not. David is using this expression to emphasize that Jonathan was as dear to him as a brother would have been.
David is saying that his bond of friendship with Jonathan meant more to him than any romantic relationship with a woman. See the discussion of this statement in the Introduction to this chapter.
1:27: David is using these weapons by association to mean Saul and Jonathan who used them so skillfully, as he describes in 1:22.
2:3: The author is using the term house by association to mean the people who lived in the same house with a man. He means the people in that man’s household.
2:4: Here, house represents all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Judah figuratively means all the people descended from Judah, one of the sons of Jacob or Israel.
2:5: The author is using the term he said by association to mean that David said this through the messengers he sent.
עֲשִׂיתֶם הַחֶסֶד הַזֶּה עִם־אֲדֹנֵיכֶם עִם־שָׁאוּל וַתִּקְבְּרוּ אֹתוֹ
This expression conveys a single idea by using two phrases connected with and. The phrase have buried him tells in what way the people have done this kindness with Saul.
2:7: David is using one part of the people of Jabesh Gilead, their hands, to mean all of them in the act of being courageous.

In certain contexts, biblical authors and characters use the expression sons of to describe people who have a certain quality. In this case, sons of valor describes warriors who have the quality of valor, which is courage in dangerous situations.
2:9: The author is making a generalization for emphasis.
2:10: In this culture, to say how old a man was, speakers would say that he was a son of a certain number of years.
The author is speaking as if the people of Judah had positioned themselves physically behind David. He means that they were loyal to him as their king.
2:11: The author is using the phrase the number of the days by association to mean the length of time, since time is made up of days.
2:13: The word Zeruiah is the name of a woman, David’s older sister.
אֵלֶּה עַל־הַבְּרֵכָה מִזֶּה וְאֵלֶּה עַל־הַבְּרֵכָה מִזֶּה
The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that the two groups were on opposite sides of the pool from each other.
2:14: While these young men would have to arise from their seated position, Abner could be using the term here to suggest that they take action. That is one frequent meaning of the term.
See the discussion of the possible meanings here of the term play in the Introduction to this chapter.
See the discussion of the term face in the Introduction to 2 Samuel.
2:16: The author is using the term head by association to mean the hair on the head.
The author is using the term fell by association to mean that they died, since they fell down when they died.

As the author indicates, Helkath Hazzurim is the name of a place. However, the exact meaning is uncertain. One possible meaning is “The Field of the Sides,” which would be an allusion to the way each soldier stabbed his opponent in the side. Another possible meaning is “The Field of the Swords” or “The Field of the Daggers,” which would be an allusion to the weapons that the soldiers used.
2:17: The author is using the term face by association to mean that Abner and the men of Israel were in front of the servants of David. The expression indicates agency. It means that David’s soldiers struck Abner and his soldiers as they engaged them in battle. See the discussion of this phrase in the Introduction to 2 Samuel.
By were struck, the author means that Abner and the men of Israel “were defeated” in battle. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to 2 Samuel.
2:18: The author is using a common expression of his culture, light on his feet, to mean that Asahel was very fast when he ran.
The word gazelles describes small, fast-running, deer-like animals.
2:19: The author is speaking of two extremes, right and left, in order to mean them and everything in between.
2:22: לָמָּה אַכֶּכָּה אַרְצָה וְאֵיךְ אֶשָּׂא פָנַי אֶל־יוֹאָב אָחִיךָ
Abner is using the question form for emphasis.
By strike you to the ground, Abner means kill Asahel, causing him to fall to the ground dead.
Abner failing to lift his face to look at Joab directly would be a symbolic action that would express shame for killing Asahel, a younger, less experienced warrior.
2:23: The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Asahel died right in the place where Abner killed him, that is, on the ground that was under him at that time. The author is not saying that Abner stood over Asahel as he was dying.
The author is making a generalization for emphasis, since the next verse shows that every did not include Joab and Abishai.
See the discussion in the Introduction to the chapter of why the soldiers who came to this place may have stood still there.
2:24: The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that the sun was setting.
The author is using the term face by association to mean that the hill of Ammah was opposite or facing the place called Giah.
2:25: The author is speaking as if these soldiers had positioned themselves physically behind Abner. He means that they were following Abner as their leader.
The author is speaking of this hill as if it were a living thing that could have had a head.
2:26: Abner is using the question form for emphasis.
Abner is speaking of a sword as if it were a living thing that could devour something.
Abner is speaking as if his soldiers were the actual brothers of Joab’s soldiers. He means they were fellow Israelites.
2:27: Following the custom of his culture, Joab is swearing an oath by guaranteeing it by something he holds sacred, The life of God.
Joab is using a common expression of his culture to mean that his soldiers would have stopped pursuing Abner’s men.
2:28: The author is using the name of a nation by association to represent its army. See the discussion of this in the Introduction to 2 Samuel.
2:31: The author is using the name of a person by association to represent his descendants, the tribe of Benjamin.
2:32: Ordinarily, soldiers were buried on the battlefield where they had died, so carrying Asahel’s body more than fifteen kilometers (more than ten miles) to his family tomb in Bethlehem was a symbolic action that showed special honor to him as a great warrior and as the brother of the commanding general, Joab.
The author is using the term it became light by association to mean that the sky had begun to become light when they reached Hebron.
3:1: In this context, the term house refers to the family line of a king, which might include several descendants who were his successors as king.

The phrases going and strong and going and weak express single ideas. The word going indicates that the strength and weakness grew greater over time.

The author is using David to represent David and all those who supported him.
3:2: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens later in the story. Three of these sons, Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah, will figure prominently in the narrative.
3:5: The author expects his readers to understand that this phrase applies to all of the women he lists here, not just to Eglah. These sons of his wives had rights of inheritance, and so they competed to succeed David as king, as much of the later story relates.)
3:7: Ishbosheth is using the question form to rebuke Abner.
Ishbosheth is referring to sexual relations in a polite way by using the phrase gone in to.
3:8: The author is describing Abner becoming extremely angry by association with the way a person’s skin may become hot when he is angry.
The author is using the term words to represent what Ishbosheth said by using words.
Abner is using one part of a dog, his head, to mean an entire dog. He may be doing this to make his statement more elaborate and emphatic.
Abner is using the question form to express anger and deny that he is worthless.
In this culture, people considered wild dogs dirty and regarded them with contempt. Abner is suggesting that the Judeans are contemptible for not supporting Saul’s son as their next king.
Here, hand represents the capability of a person.
See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of how, if Abner had actually had sexual relations with Rizpah, that would have been a symbolic action asserting a claim to be the king.
3:9: Abner swears in this verse that he is going to do something, but he does not describe until the next verse what he is going to do.
Following the custom of his culture, Abner is using a conditional statement to swear an oath. What he states as a condition (“if”) is what he is swearing to do.
כֹּה־יַעֲשֶׂה אֱלֹהִים לְאַבְנֵר וְכֹה יֹסִיף לוֹ
When Abner says thus may he add, he is using a common expression of his culture.
כֹּה־יַעֲשֶׂה אֱלֹהִים לְאַבְנֵר וְכֹה יֹסִיף לוֹ

The word Thus: (1) could refer to what Abner describes in the next verse. Abner could be saying that if he does not take away the privileged position of Saul’s family, then he wants God to take away his privileged position as a powerful leader. (2) could be a general expression introducing the entire statement as a reference to severe punishment.
3:10: Abner is using the term kingdom to mean a king’s rule over the Israelites, not the Israelites themselves over whom he would rule.
Here, Abner is speaking as if the kingdom might physically pass over from one location to another.
Abner is speaking as if he would physically raise up the throne of David to a high position above Israel and Judah.
Abner is referring to all of the Israelite territory by naming two extremes, Dan (a city in the far north) and Beersheba (a city in the far south).
3:11: The author is using the term word to represent what Ishbosheth might have said by using words.
3:12: Abner is using the question form for emphasis. Abner could mean: (1) that he, not Ishbosheth, actually controls the land, so if David makes a covenant with him, he can deliver all of Israel to David; (2) that since the Lord promised David the kingship, Abner will help him become the king of all of Israel on that basis.
Abner is using his hand to represent himself in the act of accompanying and assisting David.
In telling David he will be with him, Abner is using a common expression of his culture to mean that he will help him.
Here, Abner is speaking as if he would physically make the Israelites turn in a different direction.
3:13: David is using face to represent his whole person.
3:15: See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of why this man is called Paltiel here but Palti when he first appears in the story in 1 Samuel 25:44.
3:16: The phrase going and weeping expresses a single idea. The word weeping tells in what way Paltiel was going.

Abner could be using the term Go to tell Paltiel: (1) that he must now return. Bahurim was near the border of Judah, and Abner did not want Paltiel to enter the territory that David was ruling; (2) that Paltiel must leave that place, where Michal was, and return to his home without her.
3:17: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
The author is using the term word to represent what Abner said by using words.
Abner is using Both yesterday and the third day as a common expression of his culture to mean the way things had been previously.
3:18: Here, hand represents the actions of a person.
Here, hand represents the power or control of a group.
3:19: The author is using the term ears to mean hearing.
אֵת כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־טוֹב בְּעֵינֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבְעֵינֵי כָּל־בֵּית בִּנְיָמִן
See the discussion of the phrase good in the eyes of in the Introduction to this chapter.
Here, Israel represents the people of Israel.
3:20: Bringing a round and significant number of men with him was a symbolic action by which Abner showed respect for David.
3:21: Abner says all of Israel as an generalization for emphasis.
Abner is using David’s soul to represent all of him as a person.
3:24: Joab is using the question form to challenge David for letting Abner go.
Joab is using the question form to express his strong disapproval of David letting Abner go.
3:25: Joab is speaking of the first and last actions of a military campaign, going out and coming in, in order to mean military activities as a whole.
3:27: The author assumes that his readers will know that by the middle of the gate, he is referring to an area within the city wall between the openings that led out of the city and into the city.
Here, blood represents the killing of Asahel for which Joab wanted to take revenge.
3:28: The implication is that David is referring not just to his current reign but to the continuing rule of his descendants.
Here, blood represents the killing of Abner.
3:29: יָחֻלוּ עַל־רֹאשׁ יוֹאָב וְאֶל כָּל־בֵּית אָבִיו

David is using the same common expression here that he used in 1:16, about blood being on someone’s head, to mean that a person was morally and legally responsible for something and would be punished for it. Here he uses a more vivid form of the expression and wishes that the blood of Abner would writhe on Joab’s head. This represents the sufferings of Joab and his extended family that David describes in the rest of the verse.
The expression the house of his father refers to Joab’s extended family and descendants.

This expression could describe: (1) a person who, because of injury or illness, needs to use a staff to support himself when standing or walking; (2) a man who, because of injury or weakness, cannot do strenuous work or fight in battles and so must do domestic work such as using a distaff (spindle) to wind wool into thread.
David is using bread to represent all food or basic necessities.
3:30: The author is providing background information to help readers understand why David so greatly disapproved of what Joab had done. The author is contrasting the way Abner killed Asahel in battle (as he described in 2:23) with the way Joab and Abishai murdered Abner treacherously under peaceful conditions.
3:31: Tearing one’s clothes and wearing sackcloth were symbolic actions that showed intense grief and mourning in ancient Israelite culture.
Here David speaks of Abner to mean Abner’s body.
Here, walking behind the bier was a symbolic action by which David showed public respect for Abner and demonstrated that he had not been responsible for Abner’s death.
A bier is a kind of platform or frame used to carry a dead body to burial.
3:32: Here, the author is speaking as if voice were an object that could be lifted up.
The phrase lifted up his voice and wept expresses a single idea. The words lifted up his voice describe in what way David wept.
3:33: David is using the question form to emphasize how wrong it was for Abner to have died the way he did.
The implication is that Abner died in an unjust and dishonorable way, as if he were a criminal deserving death, when in fact he was not.
3:34: David is speaking to Abner, who is dead and cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about how Abner was treacherously murdered.
Here, bound hands and shackled feet represent being held as a prisoner.
3:35: The author says all of the people as a generalization for emphasis.
The author is using bread to represent food in general.
The word Thus: (1) could refer to the way Abner died a violent death; (2) could be a general expression introducing the entire statement as a reference to severe punishment.
David not eating bread or anything else until sunset, not even a small taste, was a symbolic action that showed deep mourning and grief in ancient Israelite culture.
3:36: כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה הַמֶּלֶךְ בְּעֵינֵי כָל־הָעָם טוֹב
The author says everything that the king did was good in the eyes of all of the people as a generalization for emphasis.
3:38: הֲלוֹא תֵדְעוּ כִּי־שַׂר וְגָדוֹל נָפַל הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
David is using the question form for emphasis when he makes a strong statement that his people should recognize Abner’s importance.
David is using the term this day to refer to a specific time.
4:1: The author is reporting that Ishbosheth’s hands dropped in order to indicate that he lost his strength and courage.
4:2: See the discussion of this statement in the Introduction to this chapter.
4:3: וַיִּבְרְחוּ הַבְּאֵרֹתִים גִּתָּיְמָה וַיִּהְיוּ־שָׁם גָּרִים עַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה

The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of why the author may provide this information.

See the discussion of this phrase in the Introduction to 2 Samuel. The author is using this phrase to refer to the time when he was writing. Avoid giving the impression the phrase means “to the present day.”
4:4: The author is speaking of the report as if it were a living thing that could have come from a place.
4:5: The phrase bed of noon describes a special bed or couch on which someone would rest or sleep during the midday rest period that was common in this region where the middle of the day would be very hot.
4:6: Following the conventions of Hebrew storytelling, the author gives a general summary of these events in this verse and then describes them in more specific detail in the next verse.
4:8: Rechab and Baanah are using this phrase to describe Saul, not Ishbosheth.
By saying that Saul sought David’s life, Rechab and Baanah mean that Saul sought to take his life, that is, to kill him.
The speaker is speaking here of descendants as if they were seed.
4:9: Following the custom of his culture, David is swearing an oath by guaranteeing it by something he holds sacred. David is using this oath to swear that what he says in the next verse is true.
4:10: In this figure of speech, David actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of his words.
4:11: הֲלוֹא אֲבַקֵּשׁ אֶת־דָּמוֹ מִיֶּדְכֶם וּבִעַרְתִּי אֶתְכֶם מִן־הָאָרֶץ
David is using the question form to emphasize that he will certainly punish Rechab and Baanah for killing Ishbosheth.
Here, David is speaking as if he would consume the murderers as fire consumes something completely. This image emphasizes total destruction.
4:12: This could mean: (1) that David’s soldiers hung up the hands and feet of Rechab and Baanah beside the pool. This would have been a symbolic action, exposing to disgrace in a public location the hands that these men had used to murder Ishbosheth and the feet that they had used to flee with his head. By this action, David would have been repudiating their deed and warning others against doing anything similar. This too would have disgraced them as murderers, repudiated their deed, and warned others. However, it would have been a violation of Deuteronomy 21:23, which required the Israelites to bury the body of an executed person on the same day on which he was executed. So this is less likely.
5:1: The author is speaking of a whole, all of the tribes of Israel, to mean a part of that whole, representatives of the tribes who came to David.
Here, we are your bone and your flesh was a common expression that the tribal representatives were using to affirm to David that they were related by descent from a common ancestor.
5:2: Here the term Israel represents the Israelite soldiers whom David commanded.
אַתָּה תִרְעֶה אֶת־עַמִּי אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאַתָּה תִּהְיֶה לְנָגִיד עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵל
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.

The Lord is speaking here as if David would actually shepherd the people of Israel as though they were sheep. This image compares the way a shepherd cares for and guides his sheep to the way a king should care for and lead his people.
5:6: The Jebusites say the blind and the lame will turn you away as an extreme statement for emphasis.
5:7: The author is providing background information to explain to readers that the fortified area that he calls Zion is the same area that they know as the City of David.

20:18: The woman is quoting a proverb in order to convince Joab that the people of Abel will be able to suggest a wise solution to the problem that has led Joab to put the city under siege.
20:19: The woman is speaking on behalf of her city, saying what she believes it would say if it could talk about itself. She is actually speaking for herself and her fellow residents of the city.
The woman is speaking of Abel Beth Maacah as if it were a living thing that Joab and his soldiers could kill.
The phrase city and a mother expresses a single idea. The word mother tells what kind of city this is.
The woman is speaking of Abel Beth Maacah as if it were actually a mother in Israel.
The woman is using the question form to rebuke Joab.
The wise woman is speaking as if Joab and his soldiers would actually devour or eat up Abel Beth Maacah.

The woman is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were something that the Lord had inherited as a lasting possession. She is referring to the Israelites as the people who belong to the Lord perpetually.
20:20: Joab is using a common expression of his culture to express his horror at the idea he describes.
These two phrases if I should devour and if I should destroy mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
20:21: Joab is using me to represent himself and his soldiers.
20:22: The author is saying all of the people as a generalization for emphasis.
20:23: See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of the list that begins here and continues to the end of the chapter.
Here, the author is speaking as if these commanders had stood physically over or above their troops. He means that they commanded them.
21:1: The author is using the phrase sought the face of as a common expression in of his culture to mean “prayed to” or “asked guidance from.” In this case, David was praying to the Lord about the cause of the famine.
21:2: The author is saying the Gibeonites as a generalization. He does not mean that David spoke with the entire people group, but with some representatives of it.
Here, the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
The author assumes that readers will know that the Israelites had sworn to protect the Gibeonites and not kill them, as recorded in Joshua 9.
The author is speaking as if the people of Israel and Judah were actually the sons of the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel, and the patriarch Judah.
See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of the term strike and its past form “struck,” which mean “kill” or “killed” here and in several other places in the chapter.
21:3: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
21:4: The Gibeonites are referring to all forms of payment by naming two major forms of money in this culture, silver and gold.

The Gibeonites could mean: (1) that there is not a man (that is, there is no one) in their people group who is authorized to kill anyone in Israel. In other words, since they apparently do not have the right to execute Israelites who may have committed capital crimes against them, they are indirectly introducing a request that David execute some of Saul’s descendants. (The next sentence shows that David recognizes they are asking something of him.); (2) that the Gibeonites are making a generalization and they expect David to understand that it includes an exception.
21:5: אֲשֶׁר כִּלָּנוּ וַאֲשֶׁר דִּמָּה־לָנוּ נִשְׁמַדְנוּ מֵהִתְיַצֵּב בְּכָל־גְּבֻל יִשְׂרָאֵל
The Gibeonites are describing one event before describing another event that preceded it.
Here, border represents the territory of Israel, since that territory is defined by its border.
21:6: The Gibeonites’ request to hang Saul’s descendants was a symbolic action by which they sought to avenge themselves on Saul’s family and restore justice for the harm he had done to them. In this culture, seven was a number symbolic of completeness.
Here, the Gibeonites are speaking as if Saul’s sons were actually sons he had personally fathered. They mean his descendants, including grandsons and other male relatives.
The Gibeonites are using the common expression of their culture before the Lord to mean that the Lord would witness their act of justice.
21:8: Some other Hebrew manuscripts and some manuscripts of the Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation) read “Merab.” That was probably the original reading, since 1 Samuel 18:19 describes how it was Merab who married Adriel of Meholah, while the author says in 6:23 that Michal had no children.
21:9: Here, to the face of represents being in the presence of the Lord.
Here the term days represents a certain time, since time is made up of days.
21:10: The author assumes that readers will know that Rizpah spread this sackcloth against a rock to make a shelter for herself while she guarded the bodies of her male relatives.

Sending rain (water) from the sky (the heavens) was a symbolic action by which the Lord showed that justice had been satisfied for the crime of Saul, which had been the cause of the three-year drought and famine.
The implication is that the birds would rest or land on the dead bodies because they wanted to feed on them.
21:14: The author is using the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son also to represent the bones of Saul’s male relatives whom the Gibeonites executed.
The implication is that the servants buried the bones at the king’s command.
By this, the author means that God responded to prayers for the land only after the Gibeonites had been avenged and Saul’s descendants had been properly buried.
21:16: Here, the author is speaking of the children of Rapha as if Rapha were actually their physical father. He means they were among the descendants of Rapha, the group of giants called Raphaites.
These 300 shekels of bronze equaled about 3 ½ kilograms or nearly 8 pounds.

Some versions are more specific and say “a new sword” or “new armor.” The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation) has a term that means “a club” or “a mace” (a club with an iron coating or head). This suggests that the original text could have named some rare but formidable weapon whose name was not preserved exactly in the traditional text.
21:17: David’s men are speaking of him as if he were a lamp providing light for Israel. They mean that he was Israel’s leader who guided them as a lamp would light the way on a path.
21:18: The traditional Hebrew text reads “Gob” here. However, a place called Gob is otherwise not known. The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation) reads “Gath.” The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 20:4 reads “Gezer.” So there is some doubt as to the actual name of this place.
21:19: The traditional Hebrew text reads “Jaare Oregim” here. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 20:5 reads “Jair.” That may have been the original reading, since the word “oregim” means “weavers” and occurs later in the verse. It may have accidentally been copied here.

The traditional Hebrew text reads “Goliath the Gittite” here. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 20:5 reads “the brother of Goliath the Gittite.” That may have been the original reading, since 1 Samuel 17:1–51 describes how it was actually David who killed Goliath the Gittite.
A beam of weavers was the thick, strong beam on which weavers hung their fabric.
21:22: Here, hand represents the power and capability of David and his servants to defeat these enemies.
22:1: David is using the term day to refer to a specific time.
22:2: This verse says basically the same thing as the previous verse. See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of how Hebrew poetry was based on the repetition of words, phrases, and ideas.
The terms rock and stronghold mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis.
David is speaking here of The Lord as if he were a rock and a stronghold. He means that the Lord provides safety and protection for him.
22:3: David is speaking of God as if he were a high rock that he could climb up to reach safety from danger.
David is speaking of taking refuge in God as if God were a place of safety in which he could hide.
Here David is speaking of the Lord as if he were a shield that protected him from attack.
David is speaking of God’s power to save him as if it were a powerful horn of an animal. A horn was a symbol of strength in ancient Israelite culture because animals use their horns as weapons.
Hebrew had more synonyms for these ideas than some other languages may have.
The terms stronghold and refuge mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis.
David is speaking of the Lord as if he were a stronghold and refuge, places where people could go to be safe from their enemies.
22:5: David is speaking of death as if it were a flood with powerful waves that could surround and overwhelm him.
David speaks here of torrents of wickedness as if wickedness were a flood of rushing water that could overwhelm and destroy him.
22:6: Here, Sheol, the abode of the dead according to Hebrew culture, represents death itself.
David is speaking as if Sheol or death actually had cords that it could use to bind him. This suggests he felt trapped in a situation where he thought he would die.
David speaks here of snares of death as if death were a hunter that could set traps for people.
22:7: Here, voice represents what David used his voice to say in his prayer.
By his temple, David means God’s temple in heaven.
David is using the term ears to mean hearing.
22:8: Hebrew had more synonyms for this idea, which David also expresses with the verbs translated as trembled and quaked, than some other languages may have.
The terms shook and trembled mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis.
David is speaking as if the earth were actually a person who could shake and tremble with fear. This expresses how powerfully God responded to David’s prayer.

David assumes that people listening to this song will recognize, according to the understanding of this culture, that the phrase the foundations of the heavens refers to solid places on which the sky rested.
The terms quaked and shook themselves mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis.
22:9: David is saying that when the Lord came to help him, the Lord’s power was so great that it was like a volcano. A volcano is an opening in the earth through which gases, smoke-like ash, and very hot, liquid rock come out. The rock can cool and build up over time to form a hill or mountain. David is describing the opening at the top of a volcano, from which Smoke and fire and Coals come out, as if it were the nose and mouth of the volcano.
David is speaking of the fire that comes from a volcano, which represents God here, as if it were a wild animal that devoured its prey.
22:11: The phrase rode and flew expresses a single idea. The word flew tells more about how he rode.
David is speaking as if God were actually riding on a cherub and flying through the sky. This is part of a poetic description of God’s power and swift action to help David.
David is speaking as if the wind actually had wings and that it could fly through the sky carrying the Lord.
22:12: David is speaking as if the darkness were actually set like a physical object that could be arranged in place. He means that God caused darkness to surround himself.
The phrases a gathering of waters and clouds of the skies mean similar things. David is using the two phrases together for emphasis.
22:13: Here, before him represents being in God’s presence.

Since David says that these coals of fire came From this brightness, he does not mean that they burned in place where they were. He means that they came burning forth. Within the image of a thunderstorm, he is referring to flashes of lightning.
22:15: Here David is using an image within an image. Within the image of a thunderstorm that represents the Lord coming powerfully to help him, David speaks of lightning bolts as if they were arrows.
The pronoun them refers in each instance to David’s enemies.
22:17: Here, height represents “heaven” as God’s dwelling place.
Here, many waters represents the sea, since the sea contains much water.
Here, many waters, meaning the sea, represents deep trouble or dangerous situations. David uses this image because he had earlier described his enemies as dangerous flood waters.
22:20: Here David is speaking of being rescued as if he had been squeezed into a narrow space and God brought him out to an open space. The image suggests that David had been in a dangerous situation with no way to escape, but God enabled him to escape.
22:21: David is speaking of his actions as if they were his hands, which could be physically clean or dirty. He means that his behavior has been morally pure.
22:22: David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a way or path that the person was walking along.
22:23: David is speaking of judgments as if they were objects that could be physically placed in front of him. This means that he constantly remembers and thinks about God’s laws.
David is speaking of disobeying God’s statutes as if they were objects that he could physically turn away from. He is describing refusing to obey God’s commands.
22:25: Here, before his eyes represents how God sees and evaluates people.
22:26: The phrase mighty blameless expresses a single idea. The word mighty expresses to what degree these people are blameless.
22:27: Here David is speaking of people who deliberately do what is wrong as if they were physically crooked or bent.
22:28: וְאֶת־עַם עָנִי תּוֹשִׁיעַ וְעֵינֶיךָ עַל־רָמִים תַּשְׁפִּיל
Here David is speaking as if oppressed people were lowly, that is, in a physically low place, and as if proud people were physically high and the Lord brought them down to a lower place.
David is using eyes against to represent God’s attention and opposition.
22:29: אַתָּה נֵירִי יְהוָה וַיהוָה יַגִּיהַּ חָשְׁכִּי

Here David is speaking as if the Lord were actually a lamp that gives him light in his darkness. This image is rich in meaning. Among the meanings that come out in this context is that the Lord helps him understand what he should do when he would otherwise be confused or uncertain.
22:30: This could mean: (1) that David is saying that by God’s help, he can pursue and overtake a troop. He may be recalling how he and his men were able to overtake the Amalekite “troop” (1 Samuel 30:8) that had raided Ziklag and rescue their families and possessions; (2) that David is saying that by God’s help, he can directly attack and disperse an opposing group of soldiers.

David is speaking of successfully leading troops to capture a fortified city as if he and they would leap over its walls. He may be recalling how he and his soldiers were able to capture the stronghold of Zion in Jerusalem (5:6–9).
22:31: Here David is speaking of how God acts and directs others as if it were a way or path that he was walking along.
Here, word of the Lord represents what the Lord says by using words.
David is speaking as if God were actually a shield behind which people took refuge.
22:32: כִּי מִי־אֵל מִבַּלְעֲדֵי יְהוָה וּמִי צוּר מִבַּלְעֲדֵי אֱלֹהֵינוּ
David is using the question form for emphasis.
David speaks of God here as if God were a rock. This means that God provides safety and protection, like a large rock that people can hide behind or stand on for safety.
22:33: Here David is speaking as if God were actually a fortress of strength.

This could mean: (1) that God makes the way on which a person travels perfect, that is, free from obstacles; (2) that David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a way or path that the person was walking along.
22:34: Here David is comparing his ability to move quickly and surely with the way a deer moves in difficult terrain.
22:35: David is using his hands to represent all of him in the act of fighting in battle.
22:36: Here David is speaking of God’s power to save him as if it were a shield that could protect him from physical attacks.
By your answer, David means God’s response to his prayers requesting help.
22:37: Here, David’s step represents the place where he would step.
David is speaking as if God had made the area where he needed to walk more spacious. This represents having freedom to move and act without being constrained by enemies.
22:39: Here David is speaking of destroying his enemies as if he were a wild animal that could devour them.
David is describing one event before describing another event that preceded it.
The implication is that David’s enemies fall and remain dead.
22:40: Here David is speaking of valor as if it were a piece of clothing with which God girds him, like a belt or piece of armor.
David means that people who try to rebel against him ultimately bow down as a symbolic action by which they show renewed submission to his authority.
22:41: David is describing a symbolic action in which victorious soldiers would make defeated enemies lie face down on the ground and then step on their necks to demonstrate their complete triumph (as in Joshua 10:24, for example).
22:42: By he does not answer them, David means that the Lord does not help his enemies as they have asked.
22:43: The point of this comparison is that just as the dust of the earth consists of tiny pieces, so, in this image, David beat his enemies so thoroughly that they broke into small pieces.
David speaks here of defeating his enemies as if he had actually beaten them into small pieces. This compares his total victory over his enemies to the way that dust can be completely scattered.
Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were mud that he could crush and trample. This metaphor emphasizes his complete victory over them.
22:44: Here David is speaking of his leadership role as if he were the head of a body. Just as the head directs the rest of the body, David ruled over other nations.
22:45: In certain contexts, biblical authors and characters use the common expression of their culture Sons of to indicate that a person has a certain characteristic. In this case, these people have the characteristic of being foreigners or people from other nations.
David is using one part of a person, the ear to represent entire people in the act of hearing.
David means that these people hear specifically about him.
By they hear me, David means that they obey him.
22:46: Here David is speaking of foreign armies as if they were plants that fade away and lose their vitality.

In certain contexts, biblical authors and characters use the expression son of to indicate that a person has the characteristic of something. In this case, the people whom David is describing have the characteristic of being soldiers of foreign countries that are resisting his rule.
22:47: David is speaking of God as if he were a large rock or cliff where David could find safety from his enemies.
22:48: Here David is speaking of conquering peoples as if they were being brought down physically under his feet.
22:49: By bringing me out from my enemies, David means escaping from being confined or restrained by his enemies.
Here David is speaking of his enemies as if they were physically arising upward to attack him, and he speaks of God as physically lifting him up above them.
22:50: Here, name represents the Lord himself, in light of his fame and reputation.
22:51: Jewish scribes instructed synagogue readers to say “a tower of salvation to his king” when they got to this phrase. That could have been the original reading.
Here David is speaking of his offspring as if they were actually seed. Just as a seed can grow into a plant that produces more seeds, David’s descendants would continue to come from his family line.
23:1: נְאֻם דָּוִד בֶּן־יִשַׁי וּנְאֻם הַגֶּבֶר הֻקַם עָל
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
The author is speaking of David’s position of authority as if it were a height. He means that God gave David great power and honor.
23:2: These two clauses say basically the same thing as the previous verse. See the discussion in the Introduction to chapter 22 of how Hebrew poetry was based on the repetition of words, phrases, and ideas.
David is using the term word to represent what he said by using words.
David is using his tongue to represent all of himself in the act of speaking.
23:4: The point of this comparison is that just as the light of morning is beneficial and brings blessing, so does a righteous ruler.
23:5: David is using the question form to make a strong statement about how God has blessed his family.

As in 1:12 and similar contexts, house here means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. In this specific context, David is using the term house to mean his dynasty, his royal line of descendants who would rule after him.
David is using the question form to emphasize that God will certainly do what he is describing.
Here David is speaking of his salvation and desire as if they were plants that God would cause to grow.
23:6: The point of this comparison is that just as thorns are worthless and thrown away, so are the wicked.
23:7: Here, wood of a spear represents the shaft or handle of a spear.
23:8: The author is using the image of the head to represent leadership.
23:9: The author assumes that his readers will know that by there, he means Pas Dammim, a place where the Israelites and Philistines frequently fought battles.
The author is using taunting the Philistines, the first thing that the Israelites did in this battle, to represent everything they did in the entire battle.
By went up, the author means the Israelite soldiers retreated to higher ground away from the battle.
23:10: By struck the Philistines, the author means that Eleazar killed Philistine soldiers. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to 2 Samuel.
The author seems to be using he word hand in its first instance to represent the power of a person.
23:11: The author is using the phrase full of lentils as a common expression of his culture to mean that there were lentils that had been planted and had grown up and ripened in this part of the field of battle.
The author is using the face of the Philistines to represent running their presence.
23:12: The author is describing one event before describing another event that preceded it.
By struck, the author means in this context that he killed Philistine soldiers in battle. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to 2 Samuel.
23:13: The author is using the image of the head to mean a leader or chief.
The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 11:15 reads “the rock.” That may have been the original reading, since it suits the grammar and context better and involves a difference of only one letter.
23:15: מִי יַשְׁקֵנִי מַיִם מִבֹּאר בֵּית־לֶחֶם אֲשֶׁר בַּשָּׁעַר
David is using the question form to express his strong desire for water from the well.
23:16: The pouring out of the water was a symbolic action by which David showed that this water, obtained at great risk by his men, was too precious to drink, and it deserved to be offered to the Lord instead.
23:17: David is speaking as if the water that the men brought were actually their blood. He means that the water represents the danger into which these men put their lives to get it for him.
23:18: The author is identifying Abishai as the brother of Joab and the son of Zeruiah. (Joab was also the son of Zeruiah, but the author is making clear that Zeruiah was the mother of Abishai. She could have been the mother of Joab without being the mother of Abishai.) Abishai was Joab’s younger brother.
The word Zeruiah is the name of a woman, David’s older sister.

The author seems to be describing two different groups of three warriors. Some versions express the interpretation that Abishai was the commander of the Three, that is, the great warriors of the first rank. Other versions follow some ancient manuscripts and say that Abishai was the commander of the Thirty, the warriors listed in 23:24–39.
The author is using the image of the head to represent a leader or commander.
23:19: The author is using the question form for emphasis to affirm that Abishai was indeed the most honored of the three.

Here, come to represents joining or achieving the same level of status as the Three. The verse means that although Abishai was a great warrior and was highly honored, he did not achieve membership in or equal status with the Three.
23:20: In certain contexts, biblical authors and characters use the expression son of to indicate that a person has the characteristic of something. In this case, the author is saying that Benaiah has the characteristic of valor.
Interpreters do not understand exactly what the term Ariel means. However, many interpreters believe that it may be describing warrior champions as lion-like, that is, strong and fierce.
23:21: The author is using a man of appearance as a common expression of his culture to mean a giant.
The author seems to mean that Benaiah went down from the Israelite battle lines on a safe height, and he went into a valley to fight this man of Egypt in single combat between the battle lines.
23:32: It is possible that here the author is using the plural term sons to introduce a single individual, as in Genesis 46:23, “And the sons of Dan, Hushim.”
23:33: Since the author lists Shammah the Hararite as one of the Three greatest warriors in 23:11–12, his name seems out of place in this list of the Thirty. Some interpreters suggest that the explanation is that the Jonathan mentioned in the previous verse was his son. Some versions accordingly read, at the end of the previous verse and the beginning of this one, “Jonathan the son of Shammah the Hararite.” The reading in 1 Chronicles 11:34 suggests this as a possible reading.
23:39: The total of 37 warriors seems to be the sum of the thirty-one listed in 23:24–39, described as the Thirty, and those said to be greater than these Thirty, that is, the Three described in 23:11–12 and the three described in (23:13–23) (although one of them is not named).
24:2: This seems to be a reference to the corps of soldiers stationed at the court who always remained on active military duty, that is, to David’s permanent army. The author describes these troops in 15:18 and 20:7, and he says in 8:16 that Joab commanded them. David wanted to know how many further men were eligible for military service, that is, how great were his reserves.
By the people, in this context David means the men who could serve in his army.
24:3: Joab is using David’s eyes to represent all of him in the act of seeing.
וַאדֹנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ לָמָּה חָפֵץ בַּדָּבָר הַזֶּה
Joab is using the question form to politely express his disapproval of David’s plan to count the people.
24:4: וַיֶּחֱזַק דְּבַר־הַמֶּלֶךְ אֶל־יוֹאָב וְעַל שָׂרֵי הֶחָיִל
Here, the word of the king represents what King David said by using words.
וַיֶּחֱזַק דְּבַר־הַמֶּלֶךְ אֶל־יוֹאָב וְעַל שָׂרֵי הֶחָיִל
The author is speaking of this word as if it had been a living thing that prevailed in a contest against Joab and the commanders.
Here, to the face of represents being in the presence of a person.
24:9: The author is using this phrase, drawing the sword, to mean soldiers, by association with the way that soldiers at this time drew swords in order to fight battles.
24:10: Here, the heart represents a person’s thoughts, feelings, and conscience. When the author says that David’s heart struck him, he means that David came to feel guilty about what he had done.
24:12: The Lord is speaking of the three choices of punishment as if they were objects he could lift and hold over David. This is a metaphor that indicates that the Lord is presenting these choices to David and has authority over how they will be carried out.
24:13: The implication is that Gad declared to David the three choices that the Lord had given him, as stated in the previous verse.
Here, to the face of represents David being in front of his enemies.
Gad is speaking of a message or reply as if it were a word that was an object he could carry back to the Lord.
24:14: Here, hand represents the capability of a person. In this case, it refers to the Lord’s power to punish and his ability to show mercy.
24:16: The author could be using the same expression that occurs earlier in the book, in 1:14 and 18:12, to mean that the angel was preparing to use violence (in the form of this plague) against the people of the city of Jerusalem. When the Lord tells him to lower his hand, that could mean that he is not to afflict the people with the plague. However, since David sees the angel, it seems more likely that the angel actually had reached out and upward with his hand and that the Lord told him to put his hand back down and not use it to cause the plague.
24:17: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
David is using the question form to emphasize that the people of Israel were innocent and had done nothing wrong.
David is speaking of his subjects as if they were sheep. He means that they are innocent and defenseless, like sheep who depend on their shepherd to protect them.
Here, hand represents God’s power to punish.
24:19: Here, word represents what Gad said to David.
24:24: These 50 shekels of silver weighed about 570 grams or 1.25 pounds.
